entities.name: Owner
entities.tagline: The seat that decides what the company is for, takes the money and the liability, and says the last word on every page.

sections.heading: What it takes
sections.text: The model, read before deciding: the vision, the objectives and the strategies under them, and the values a decision is weighed against. A draft or a pull request to review, on the branch and on the rendered page. The signals a strategy names as showing whether it is working.

sections.heading: What it produces
sections.text: Decisions, recorded where they bind: a merge, a tag, a release, a signed contract, a corrected model. The proposals and pitches the company lives on, and the advice a client pays for, since in a company of one the seat that decides is the seat that sells and delivers. The reviewed English every translation is made from. The word that ends a question an agent has parked.

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text:
- Never lets a made thing outlive a disagreement with the model; the model is corrected and
  the thing rebuilt.
- Never delegates a merge, a tag or a signature; an agent opens and reports, the Owner merges.
- Never states a number that was not counted or a claim the model does not hold.

entities.name: Planner
entities.tagline: The seat that cuts an approved specification into task briefs, each whole on its own, and writes none of them.

sections.heading: What it takes
sections.text: A specification the Owner has approved, and the repository the work lands in, including the rules that bind it.

sections.heading: What it produces
sections.text: An ordered set of task briefs. Each is the whole of its own requirements, names the interfaces the briefs around it produce and consume, and states how its holder can tell it is done. The order is the order they can be worked in, not the order they were thought of.

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text:
- Never re-opens a decision the specification took.
- Never writes a brief that depends on a conversation its holder did not have.
- Never writes the change.
- Never plans a task whose completion cannot be checked.

entities.name: Reviewer
entities.tagline: The seat that reads one diff against its brief, returns findings with a severity and changes nothing.

sections.heading: What it takes
sections.text: The brief the work was done from, the implementer's report read as unverified claims, the diff as one file with its commits and context, and the constraints that bind the task.

sections.heading: What it produces
sections.text: Two verdicts, spec compliance and quality, and findings each with a file and a line, what is wrong, why it matters and how to fix it, ranked by severity, with the strengths named first. A finding is an input to whoever merges and never a verdict: it does not decide, and it is not passed on a person.

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text:
- Never mutates the working tree, the index, a branch or the pull request.
- Never re-runs a suite to confirm a report; it runs one focused test on a doubt the report
  does not answer.
- Never spawns another reviewer.
- Never marks polish as critical.

entities.name: Specifier
entities.tagline: The seat that turns a shaped request into a specification nobody has to guess at, and builds nothing.

sections.heading: What it takes
sections.text: A request already classified, the model it must not contradict, and the code or the pages it will touch, read rather than remembered. Where the request is ambiguous the seat asks before writing.

sections.heading: What it produces
sections.text: A specification that is the whole of the requirements: the gap it closes, the approaches considered with the one chosen and why, the decisions taken, and what is explicitly not being done. Where a decision is the Owner's, the seat names the options and parks the question.

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text:
- Never writes the change it specifies.
- Never decides scope; it names the options and the Owner chooses.
- Never leaves a question unasked because an assumption would be convenient.
- Never states a fact the model does not hold.

entities.name: Translator
entities.tagline: The seat that makes the Swiss Standard German of an element whose English the Owner has reviewed, and hands back a back-translation beside it.

sections.heading: What it takes
sections.text: The reviewed English of the elements the task names, and the glossary. Reviewed means the Owner has said the English is done; a draft is not reviewed, and the seat says so. Where the task names no elements, the seat names the gap and writes nothing.

sections.heading: What it produces
sections.text: The German in the element's own place, Swiss Standard German, de-CH, in the forms Switzerland uses, and beside each element a back-translation in English, so a reviewer with a minute can read what the German says.

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text:
- Never translates a draft.
- Never edits the English.
- Never writes a family term in any form but the glossary's.
- Never commits.

entities.name: Visitor
entities.tagline: Someone who asks about the company in their own words, on its site or through an agent of their own, and is owed what the model says and nothing else.

sections.heading: What it takes
sections.text: A question, in whatever words and language they have. Nothing else: the seat is filled by whoever turns up, and nobody is asked who they are.

sections.heading: What it produces
sections.text: A question, and where the answer sends them, a click on the entity it rests on: on the model page, or on the file at the commit it was read from.

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text:
- Never has to know the model's vocabulary to be answered; meeting their words is the company's work.
- Never leaves anything behind: the conversation lives in their tab and ends with it.

entities.name: Writer
entities.tagline: The seat that drafts English in the family voice from a brief, so the Owner reviews a draft instead of writing one.

sections.heading: What it takes
sections.text: A brief naming the audience, the one point, the facts the text may claim and where each is shown, and the file and the place the text lands. The rulebook and the glossary. Where the brief lacks the audience, the point or a fact's source, the seat names the gap and writes nothing.

sections.heading: What it produces
sections.text: The text in its file on the current branch, in the register the place calls for, and a reply naming what was written, what changed and which claims could not be traced to the brief or the repository.

sections.heading: What it never does
sections.text:
- Never writes a fact or a number the brief or the repository does not show.
- Never writes German; the translation is the Translator's, made after the English is
  reviewed.
- Never commits and never runs the build.
- Never uses an adjective that sells.

entities.name: Agentic AI development
entities.tagline: Building software systems in which an AI model plans and takes multi-step actions toward a goal, often using tools, with limited step-by-step human direction.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Design the goals, tools and guardrails an AI agent can use to complete a task autonomously. Build the loop that lets the agent plan, act, observe results and adjust its next action. Test for failure modes specific to autonomous behavior, such as getting stuck in loops or taking unintended actions, and add safeguards to contain them.

entities.name: Agile delivery
entities.tagline: Running iterative, incremental delivery using frameworks such as Scrum, Kanban or SAFe to organize team work.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Facilitate the planning, review and retrospective events that structure iterative delivery. Manage a backlog, track flow or velocity and remove impediments that block the team. Adapt the chosen framework's ceremonies and artifacts to fit the team and the scale of the work. Typical tools: Jira, Azure DevOps, Trello.

entities.name: AI governance
entities.tagline: The decision rights, policies and oversight under which a company uses AI.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Define who may deploy which kind of AI system for which purpose, and under what human oversight. Set the guardrails for data use, model providers and cost, and the review that checks they hold. Keep the record regulators and customers will ask for, and adjust the rules when the law or the technology changes.

entities.name: AI strategy
entities.tagline: Deciding where and how a company adopts AI, and the sequence, investment and capabilities that get it there.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Assess which business activities AI can change materially and which it cannot yet. Set the direction for adoption across plan, change and run, with the platforms, data and skills it requires. Choose between building, buying and partnering per use case, and revisit the choices as the models and the market move.

entities.name: AI tool integration (MCP)
entities.tagline: Connecting AI models and agents to external tools, data sources and systems through a standardized protocol so the AI can take real actions.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Build or configure servers that expose a system's capabilities as tools an AI agent can call. Define the interface, permissions and error handling for each exposed tool so the agent can use it safely. Test how the agent selects and sequences tool calls and adjust the tool definitions to make behavior more predictable. Typical tools: Model Context Protocol (MCP).

entities.name: API design
entities.tagline: Designing the interfaces that let software systems and services exchange data and functionality.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Define the resources, operations and data contracts an interface exposes and document them so consumers can integrate against them. Make decisions about versioning, error handling and consistency that keep the interface usable as it evolves. Review real usage patterns and feedback from consumers to refine the design over time. Typical tools: REST, GraphQL, OpenAPI.

entities.name: Business architecture
entities.tagline: Modeling an organization's capabilities, value streams and operating structures independent of the technology that supports them.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Identify and map the capabilities, value streams and organizational structures a business relies on. Use those models to assess where capabilities are duplicated, missing or misaligned with strategy. Connect the business view to technology and process decisions so investment targets the right capabilities.

entities.name: Business process modeling (BPMN, DMN)
entities.tagline: Diagramming business processes and decision logic using standardized notations so they can be analyzed, communicated and automated.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Map process flows and decision rules using notations such as BPMN for process steps and DMN for decision logic. Work with process owners to validate that the model reflects how work actually happens rather than how it is assumed to happen. Use the resulting models to identify inefficiencies or to hand off to process automation tooling. Typical tools: BPMN, DMN, Camunda.

entities.name: Change management
entities.tagline: Planning and guiding an organization through the human side of a transition so new ways of working actually take hold.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Assess the impact of a change on affected groups and build a plan to communicate, train and support them through it. Identify sources of resistance and work with sponsors and managers to address them. Track adoption after go-live and reinforce the change until it becomes the new normal.

entities.name: CI/CD
entities.tagline: Automating the build, test and release steps that take a code change from commit to running in an environment.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Configure pipelines that build and test code automatically on every change and gate progression on those results. Automate packaging and deployment so releases happen consistently and can be repeated or rolled back reliably. Monitor pipeline health and adjust stages as the codebase, tests or release process change. Typical tools: Jenkins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI.

entities.name: Cloud architecture
entities.tagline: Designing systems that run on cloud infrastructure, using its services and elasticity rather than fixed, self-managed hardware.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Select cloud services and design patterns that meet a system's scalability, resilience and cost requirements. Design for elasticity, fault tolerance across availability zones or regions and secure use of managed services. Review cost and usage patterns to right-size the architecture as workloads change. Typical tools: AWS, Azure, Google Cloud Platform.

entities.name: Community building
entities.tagline: Making a place where practitioners teach each other, and keeping it alive after the founding energy is gone.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Start with a recurring occasion — a meetup, a working group, a community of practice — and a reason to come that is not you. Hand roles to members early so the group survives your absence. Connect the community outward, to the projects, vendors and standards bodies it depends on, and measure it by what members do for each other.

entities.name: Company vision and strategy
entities.tagline: Where a company is going and why, and the few bets that get it there.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Say what the company is for in a sentence people repeat without you. Choose the markets, products and capabilities it will commit to, and name the ones it will not. Turn the choice into a plan with owners, money and dates, and read the market back into it every quarter. Carry the vision into hiring, funding and partnership conversations until it is the company's, not the founders'.

entities.name: Consulting
entities.tagline: Advising clients or internal stakeholders on how to address a problem, drawing on structured analysis and outside perspective.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Diagnose a client's problem through structured analysis, interviews and data review. Develop and present recommendations, weighing options against the client's constraints and priorities. Support the client through implementation or handoff, adjusting recommendations as new information emerges.

entities.name: Container orchestration (Kubernetes)
entities.tagline: Managing the deployment, scaling and healing of containerized applications across a cluster of machines.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Define how containerized workloads are packaged, scheduled and scaled across a cluster. Configure networking, storage and access controls that let services run reliably alongside each other. Monitor cluster health and respond to failures so workloads recover automatically rather than needing manual intervention. Typical tools: Kubernetes, Helm, Docker.

entities.name: Context engineering
entities.tagline: Structuring what an AI model or agent is given to work with — the documents, definitions and rules in its context — so its output is grounded in how the organization actually works.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Decide what an agent needs to know for a task and shape it into something a model can load: curated documents rather than raw dumps, explicit definitions rather than implied ones, rules written where the work happens. Keep the context where the people who own the facts can edit it, so it stays true without becoming a maintenance project of its own. Package and distribute it so every assistant works from the same version instead of a private copy. Test what the model does when context is missing or stale, and constrain it so a gap surfaces as a failure rather than as an invention.

entities.name: Conversational AI
entities.tagline: Systems that hold a dialogue with customers or staff across several channels, increasingly with an AI agent answering rather than a person.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Decide whether to build the conversational layer or integrate a specialist vendor, and design the boundary either way: which channels are unified, what the AI may answer on its own, and when a person takes over. Feed it the messaging history, identity and operational data it needs to answer specifically rather than generically. Keep the handover visible in one inbox so no conversation is dropped between the agent and the staff member. Watch what it does at the edge of what it knows, and make it escalate rather than guess.

entities.name: Data engineering
entities.tagline: Building the pipelines and infrastructure that move and transform data so it is reliably available for analysis or downstream systems.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Design and build pipelines that extract, transform and load data from source systems into storage or analytics platforms. Handle data quality, schema changes and failure recovery so downstream consumers can trust the data they receive. Optimize pipelines for throughput, cost and freshness as data volumes and requirements grow. Typical tools: Apache Spark, Airflow, dbt.

entities.name: Data governance
entities.tagline: Defining ownership, quality standards and policies for data so it stays trustworthy and consistent across an organization.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Define who owns and is accountable for different data domains and set standards for quality, definitions and lifecycle. Establish policies for access, retention and use of data, including master or reference data that many systems share. Run processes that monitor data quality and resolve inconsistencies across systems.

entities.name: Data modeling
entities.tagline: Representing the structure and meaning of an organization's data through conceptual, logical or physical models.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Define the entities, attributes and relationships that describe the data an organization holds. Build models at different levels of abstraction, from conceptual business terms to physical schema, and keep them consistent with each other. Review and update models as the organization's data and understanding of it evolve.

entities.name: Data protection (GDPR)
entities.tagline: Ensuring an organization's handling of personal data complies with data protection law and respects individuals' privacy rights.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Assess how personal data is collected, used and stored and identify where processing needs a legal basis or additional safeguards. Run or support data protection impact assessments and maintain records of processing activities. Handle data subject requests and breach notifications and advise other parts of the organization on compliant data handling.

entities.name: Database design
entities.tagline: Structuring how data is organized, related and constrained within a database so it supports an application's needs efficiently and correctly.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Model entities, relationships and constraints and turn them into a schema that supports the application's queries. Make trade-offs between normalization, performance and flexibility based on how the data will be read and written. Review and adjust the schema as usage patterns or requirements change.

entities.name: DevOps
entities.tagline: Bringing development and operations work together so software is built, tested, released and run as one continuous flow.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Build and maintain the automation, tooling and shared practices that let development and operations teams collaborate on the same pipeline. Work to shorten the cycle between writing code and running it reliably in production, often owning both the build process and aspects of live operation. Use feedback from production, such as incidents or performance data, to improve the development process itself. Typical tools: Docker, Kubernetes, GitHub Actions.

entities.name: Domain-driven design
entities.tagline: Structuring software around the business domain's own concepts and language rather than around technical layers.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Work with domain experts to build a shared vocabulary and model of the business domain. Identify bounded contexts and use them to draw system and team boundaries that mirror the domain's natural divisions. Keep the code's structure and terminology aligned with that domain model as understanding deepens.

entities.name: Domain-specific language design
entities.tagline: A language built for one domain — its metamodel, syntax and semantics — so that experts can state their intent directly and tools can act on it.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Identify the concepts a domain's experts actually reason in and fix them as a metamodel. Give the language a concrete syntax, textual or graphical, with the constraints that make an invalid model unwritable. Build the editor, validation and generators around it, and evolve the language with the domain without breaking existing models. Typical tools: EMF, Ecore, Xtext, Sirius, MPS.

entities.name: Engineering leadership
entities.tagline: Leading and growing software engineering organizations, balancing technical direction with people and delivery outcomes.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Set technical direction and standards across one or more engineering teams and grow the organization's structure to match. Hire, coach and develop engineers and managers, and build the processes that let teams deliver reliably at scale. Balance long-term technical investment against short-term delivery pressure and represent engineering priorities to the rest of the organization.

entities.name: Enterprise architecture
entities.tagline: Designing the structure of an organization's business capabilities, information and technology so they work together as one coherent system.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Map current business capabilities, data and technology landscapes and define target-state architectures that close identified gaps. Set architecture principles and standards that guide individual projects and technology choices. Review proposed initiatives for alignment with the target architecture and adjust it as strategy or constraints change.

entities.name: Event-driven architecture
entities.tagline: Designing systems where components communicate by producing and reacting to events rather than through direct calls.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Identify the events that matter to a system and design the producers, consumers and channels that carry events between them. Make decisions about ordering, delivery guarantees and how components stay decoupled while still working together. Design for failure modes specific to asynchronous systems, such as duplicate or out-of-order events. Typical tools: Kafka, RabbitMQ, AWS EventBridge.

entities.name: Event streaming
entities.tagline: Building systems that publish, transport and consume continuous streams of events in near real time.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Design topics or streams, partitioning and retention policies that fit how data will be produced and consumed. Build producers and consumers that handle ordering, delivery guarantees and backpressure correctly. Monitor stream throughput and lag to catch consumers falling behind before it affects downstream systems. Typical tools: Kafka, Kinesis, Pulsar.

entities.name: FinOps
entities.tagline: Managing cloud and technology spend so cost stays visible, accountable and aligned with the value delivered.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Track cloud and technology spend against budgets and attribute it to the teams or products responsible. Identify opportunities to reduce waste, such as underused resources or inefficient pricing commitments, and work with engineering teams to act on them. Build reporting and forecasts that let the organization make informed trade-offs between cost and performance. Typical tools: AWS Cost Explorer, CloudHealth, Kubecost.

entities.name: Frontend development
entities.tagline: Building user-facing web applications out of components, in whatever the browser platform has settled on at the time.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Build user interface components and manage application state so the interface reflects underlying data correctly. Choose a framework for the work in front of you and follow it where it goes, including into a version or a language that a later one replaces, and structure code so components remain reusable and testable. Reach for static typing where it catches errors before runtime. Optimize rendering performance and handle browser compatibility and accessibility concerns as the application grows. Typical tools: React, Angular, AngularJS, TypeScript, Ionic, Redux.

entities.name: Identity and access management
entities.tagline: Controlling who can authenticate to systems and what they are authorized to do once inside.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Design and configure authentication and authorization mechanisms, including protocols such as OAuth or OIDC, that verify identity and grant access. Define roles, permissions and access policies and review them to keep access aligned with actual need. Investigate access-related incidents and remove or adjust access as roles change. Typical tools: OAuth, OIDC, Okta.

entities.name: Incident management
entities.tagline: Detecting, responding to and resolving disruptions to a service so normal operation is restored as quickly as possible.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Triage incoming alerts to assess severity and impact and coordinate the people needed to investigate and restore service. Communicate status to affected stakeholders throughout the incident and decide when it can be declared resolved. Run or contribute to a post-incident review that captures root cause and follow-up actions.

entities.name: Information security management
entities.tagline: Establishing and operating a management system that identifies, treats and monitors information security risk across an organization.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Identify information assets and assess the risks they face, then define policies and controls to treat those risks. Run an ongoing management system, such as one aligned to ISO 27001, that includes audits, incident handling and continuous improvement. Report security posture and residual risk to leadership and adjust controls as threats or the organization change.

entities.name: Infrastructure as code
entities.tagline: Defining and provisioning infrastructure through versioned, executable configuration rather than manual setup.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Write declarative or scripted definitions of infrastructure and apply them through an automated pipeline. Version those definitions alongside application code and review changes before they reach live environments. Use the same definitions to reproduce environments consistently and to roll back when a change causes problems. Typical tools: Terraform, CloudFormation, Pulumi.

entities.name: Integration architecture
entities.tagline: Designing how disparate systems and applications connect and exchange data across an organization.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Map the systems that need to exchange data and design the integration patterns, message formats and middleware that connect them. Decide between approaches such as point-to-point connections, an enterprise service bus or event-based integration based on the scale and coupling required. Design for failure handling, data consistency and monitoring across integration points.

entities.name: IoT architecture
entities.tagline: Designing the path from a physical device to a business system: sensing, connectivity, ingestion, use.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Choose the sensing and the radio for the device's power, range and cost, not for the demo. Design the ingestion so that unreliable, bursty telemetry becomes a clean stream the business systems can consume. Prototype with real devices in the real environment before committing to a platform. Typical tools: LoRaWAN, RFID, MQTT.

entities.name: IT governance
entities.tagline: Establishing decision rights, policies and oversight structures that keep IT activity accountable and aligned with organizational objectives.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Define who can make which technology decisions and set the policies, standards and controls those decisions must follow. Run governance forums that review risk, compliance and investment choices, and track adherence to agreed frameworks. Adjust the governance structure as the organization and its regulatory context evolve.

entities.name: IT strategy
entities.tagline: Setting a multi-year direction for IT investment and architecture that aligns with business goals.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Assess market and technology trends, current capability gaps and business priorities to set a forward-looking direction for technology investment. Translate that direction into principles, roadmaps and target architectures that guide subsequent decisions. Engage executive stakeholders to secure buy-in and funding, and revisit the strategy as conditions change.

entities.name: Java
entities.tagline: Building software using the Java programming language and its surrounding ecosystem of libraries and runtime.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Write and maintain Java code, applying its object-oriented features and concurrency model to solve application problems. Use the surrounding ecosystem, such as build tools, frameworks and libraries, to structure and package applications. Tune and debug applications running on the Java virtual machine, including memory and performance issues specific to that runtime. Typical tools: Spring, Maven, JUnit.

entities.name: Knowledge management
entities.tagline: Capturing, organizing and sharing an organization's knowledge so it remains accessible and useful beyond the individuals who created it.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Capture knowledge from people and projects and organize it so others can find and reuse it. Design processes and tools that make contributing and searching knowledge easy enough that people actually do it. Review content over time for accuracy and relevance and retire or update material that has gone stale.

entities.name: Legacy modernization
entities.tagline: Bringing a system built for another era forward without stopping the business that runs on it.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Wrap the legacy system in a stable interface before touching its inside. Generate rather than hand-write the bridging code where the interfaces are numerous and regular. Replace one layer at a time, keeping the old path alive until the new one has carried production load.

entities.name: Machine learning
entities.tagline: Building models that learn patterns from data and use them to make predictions or decisions on new data.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Prepare and explore data, select and train models and evaluate them against relevant performance metrics. Tune model architecture and hyperparameters and validate results against held-out data to avoid overfitting. Monitor deployed models for drift or degraded performance and retrain as needed.

entities.name: Mentoring and coaching
entities.tagline: Growing other people's judgment and skill on purpose, one conversation and one review at a time.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Give people problems slightly beyond them and stay close enough that failing is safe. Ask before telling, and tell when asking would waste their week. Review work for the thinking behind it, not only the result, and say what was good as precisely as what was not. Build the places — communities of practice, pairing, retrospectives — where people teach each other without you.

entities.name: Microservices architecture
entities.tagline: Designing a system as a set of independently deployable services organized around business capabilities.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Decompose a system into services with clear boundaries and define how those services communicate and share data. Design for independent deployment, resilience to partial failure and observability across service boundaries. Weigh the added operational complexity against the flexibility gained from decoupling services. Typical tools: Kubernetes, Docker, Istio.

entities.name: MLOps
entities.tagline: Operating the pipelines and infrastructure that take machine learning models from training into reliable production use.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Build pipelines that automate data preparation, training, validation and deployment of models. Version models, data and experiments so results are reproducible, and monitor deployed models for performance and drift. Coordinate rollbacks and retraining when a model's behavior degrades in production. Typical tools: MLflow, Kubeflow, SageMaker.

entities.name: Model-driven engineering
entities.tagline: Using formal models as the primary artifact of software development, generating code or other artifacts from them rather than writing them by hand.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Define metamodels or domain-specific languages that capture a problem in a structured, formal way. Build or configure generators that transform those models into code, configuration or documentation. Keep the models as the source of truth, regenerating downstream artifacts as the models change rather than editing generated output directly.

entities.name: Multi-tenant SaaS architecture
entities.tagline: Designing a software system so a single deployment serves many customers securely and efficiently while keeping their data and usage isolated.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Decide how tenants share or are isolated from underlying compute, storage and configuration. Design for per-tenant data isolation, customization and scaling so one tenant's usage cannot affect another's experience. Plan onboarding, billing and upgrade paths that work across the whole tenant base rather than one customer at a time.

entities.name: Observability
entities.tagline: Instrumenting systems so their internal state can be understood from the data they produce, and using that data to detect and diagnose issues.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Instrument applications and infrastructure to emit logs, metrics and traces that reveal what is happening inside a system. Build dashboards and alerts that surface meaningful signals and reduce noise from irrelevant ones. Use that telemetry to diagnose the root cause of incidents and to spot degradation before it becomes an outage. Typical tools: Prometheus, Grafana, Datadog.

entities.name: Open-source stewardship
entities.tagline: Running a public project so that strangers can adopt it, contribute to it and trust it to stay.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Choose the license for the outcome you want and say what is open and what could ever be paid for. Write the README for the adopter, the conventions for the contributor and the spec for the person who will disagree with you later. Release on a contract — versions, tags, a manifest — so that nobody depends on a moving target. Keep the decisions and the rejected alternatives in the repository, where the next maintainer can find them.

entities.name: Organization design
entities.tagline: Deciding how a growing company divides its work, its decisions and its people.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Draw the teams around the products or domains they own, not around the technologies they use. Decide what a team may decide alone and what needs the room. Design for the next size, not the current one — including where a distributed or near-shore team fits — and recruit and develop the leaders each new shape requires.

entities.name: Platform engineering
entities.tagline: Building internal platforms and tooling that let product teams self-service infrastructure and common capabilities without depending on a central operations team.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Design and build the golden paths, templates and self-service tools that other engineering teams use to provision infrastructure and deploy applications. Gather requirements from those internal teams and treat the platform itself as a product with its own roadmap. Balance standardization, which reduces support burden, against flexibility for teams with unusual needs.

entities.name: Process orchestration
entities.tagline: Coordinating the execution of multi-step business processes across systems and services using a dedicated orchestration engine.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Model processes as executable workflows and configure an engine to run, track and recover them across their lifecycle. Integrate process steps with the underlying systems and services that perform the actual work. Monitor running process instances and handle failures or exceptions so processes complete correctly. Typical tools: Camunda, Zeebe, AWS Step Functions.

entities.name: Product discovery
entities.tagline: Finding out whether a product should exist before building it — the problem, the buyer, the price, the no.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Write the idea down as a claim that can be wrong: who has the problem, what they pay for today, what would make them switch. Put the smallest real thing in front of them — a talk, a model, a worked example — and collect the objections rather than the compliments. Set the outcome you will accept before you start, including a clean no, and publish what you learned either way.

entities.name: Product management
entities.tagline: Defining what a product should do and why, and steering its development to deliver value to users and the business.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Gather user and market insight to define product vision, priorities and roadmap. Translate that vision into requirements and backlog items, working closely with design and engineering to ship increments. Track outcomes after release and adjust priorities based on what is learned.

entities.name: Public speaking
entities.tagline: Explaining technical work to a room so that people leave able to act on it.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Pick the one idea the audience should take home and build the talk backward from it. Show the real system, the real numbers and the real mistake, not the slide version. Rehearse until the timing is yours, then leave room for the questions that tell you what landed.

entities.name: Requirements engineering
entities.tagline: Eliciting, documenting and managing what a system or change needs to do so that stakeholders and delivery teams share the same understanding.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Elicit needs from stakeholders through interviews, workshops or observation and turn them into clear, testable requirements. Organize and prioritize those requirements, trace them through design and delivery and manage changes as understanding evolves. Validate delivered functionality against the original requirements to confirm the need was actually met.

entities.name: Site reliability engineering
entities.tagline: Applying engineering methods to operations so that systems meet defined reliability targets at scale.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Define service level objectives and error budgets and use them to decide when to prioritize reliability work over new features. Automate operational tasks that would otherwise require repetitive manual effort and build tooling that makes systems easier to diagnose and recover. Lead or contribute to incident response and follow up with changes that reduce the chance of recurrence.

entities.name: Software architecture
entities.tagline: Defining the high-level structure of a software system, including its components, their responsibilities and how they interact.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Decompose a system into components and define the interfaces and interactions between them. Make and document decisions about structure, technology choices and trade-offs such as performance, maintainability and scalability. Review implementation to confirm it stays consistent with the intended structure as the system evolves.

entities.name: Software engineering
entities.tagline: Designing, writing, testing and maintaining software that meets defined requirements and can be operated reliably over time.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Translate requirements into working code, choosing algorithms, data structures and patterns that fit the problem. Write automated tests, review code with peers and refactor to keep the codebase maintainable as it grows. Debug and fix defects across the lifecycle, from initial development through production support.

entities.name: Software modeling (UML, SysML, C4)
entities.tagline: Using standardized diagram notations to represent a system's structure and behavior so it can be communicated and reasoned about before or alongside implementation.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Choose a notation appropriate to the audience and purpose, such as UML for software structure, SysML for systems engineering or C4 for architecture at different zoom levels. Produce diagrams that capture components, interactions or processes and keep them consistent with the system as it evolves. Use the models to communicate design intent to other engineers or stakeholders and to reason about a design before it is built.

entities.name: Software process engineering
entities.tagline: Designing how an organization builds software — the method, the disciplines, the toolchain — and getting it adopted.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Define the disciplines, artifacts and roles a delivery process needs, and write them down where teams will find them. Replace a home-grown method with a standard one where a standard exists. Build the toolchain that makes the process the easy path, and coach teams until it is how they work rather than what they were told. Typical tools: Rational Method Composer, Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, SonarQube.

entities.name: Software testing
entities.tagline: Verifying that software behaves as intended and catching defects before they reach production.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Design test cases that cover expected behavior, edge cases and failure conditions at unit, integration or end-to-end levels. Execute those tests manually or through automation and investigate failures to distinguish real defects from flaky tests. Track coverage and defect trends to focus testing effort where risk is highest. Typical tools: JUnit, Selenium, Cypress.

entities.name: Solution architecture
entities.tagline: Designing the technical solution for a specific initiative so it meets functional and non-functional requirements within the wider technology landscape.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Translate business and functional requirements into a technical design spanning applications, integrations and infrastructure. Evaluate design options against constraints such as performance, security and cost, and choose an approach that fits the surrounding architecture. Guide implementation teams through the design and adjust it as issues surface during build.

entities.name: Solution selling
entities.tagline: Winning work by showing a client the solution to their problem before they have paid for it.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Read the tender or the brief for the problem behind the requirements. Shape a solution architecture that answers it, price it honestly and present it as the people who will build it. Lead the bid across proposal, pitch and negotiation, and walk away from work that cannot be delivered as promised.

entities.name: Spec-driven development
entities.tagline: Writing down what a system must do, and why, before any of it is built — and building only against that text.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Write the specification first: purpose, decisions, the alternatives rejected and why, what is out of scope. Get it reviewed by the people who will disagree later, then derive the plan and the tests from it rather than from the code. Keep the spec in the repository beside the code it governs and change it before changing the behavior. Let agents and people build from the same text. Typical tools: spec-kit.

entities.name: Stakeholder management
entities.tagline: Identifying, engaging and maintaining productive working relationships with the people who have an interest in or influence over an initiative.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Identify stakeholders and understand their interests, concerns and level of influence. Communicate progress, negotiate expectations and resolve conflicting priorities across those groups. Keep relationships productive over time so decisions get the input and support they need.

entities.name: Storytelling
entities.tagline: Ordering facts into a story an audience will follow, and holding it together across every piece that tells it.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Decide the one claim the whole story has to land, and cut what does not carry it. Order the pieces so each stands alone and still carries the through-line — the first earns attention, the last asks for something. Fix what may be said before drafting starts, so the shape survives a co-author or a generating tool. Keep the claim checkable, because an audience that can verify one thing will grant the rest.

entities.name: Technical writing
entities.tagline: Writing that lets a reader understand and act on a technical thing without asking the author.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Decide what the reader needs to do after reading, and cut everything that does not serve it. State decisions, the alternatives that lost and the reasons, so the text survives its author. Keep one term per concept and the same term throughout. Show the real example rather than the generic one, and read the text back as the person who was not in the room.

entities.name: UX design
entities.tagline: Designing how people use a product: what they see, in what order, and what they can do next.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Work out who uses the product and what each of them came to do, then decide the structure that serves it: which pages or screens exist, what each one is for and what leads to what. Turn that into layouts, a type scale, color and components kept in one design system, so every page is built from the same parts and reads as one product. Prefer a design that holds for content not yet written over a screen drawn for each case. Review the result where it is used, rendered at the widths and themes people have, and hold it to legibility and accessibility as it grows. Typical tools: design tokens, component libraries, Figma, browser testing.

entities.name: Vendor management
entities.tagline: Selecting, contracting and overseeing external suppliers so their delivery meets agreed commitments.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text: Evaluate and select suppliers, negotiate contracts and service levels and monitor ongoing performance against them. Manage the relationship day to day, resolving issues and renegotiating terms as needs change. Balance cost, quality and risk across the supplier base.

entities.name: Local
entities.tagline: Written and kept in this repository, which masters every page in the model. Nothing syncs it, and it issues no identifiers, so no page carries a `source-id`.

entities.name: Whoever decides about me decided from the model
entities.tagline: A client or an employer arrives having read it, and the decision rests on what the model says rather than on what I said in a room.

sections.heading: What it makes true
sections.text:
The conversation starts in the wrong place today. Someone deciding whether to hire me or to buy help spends the first hour establishing what I have done, from a CV I wrote about myself, and the model — which holds the same facts with their evidence attached, and is public — is reached only if they go looking. When this holds, that hour goes to their company instead, because the background question was answered before the call.

It holds when the answer survives the check. A claim in the model names the document it rests on, so a decider can verify it without asking me, and what they verify is the same thing a search engine and an agent would have told them. That is the whole of the vision, pointed at the one moment where being true everywhere costs something if it is not.

What falls outside: how many people arrive, and whether they decide yes. This is not a reach target and no volume makes it truer — a single decision made from the model and against me satisfies it, and a room full of people who enjoyed the conversation does not. Also outside: the decisions I make about them. What I need in order to choose well is a different question and nothing here serves it.

entities.name: Model-First Strategy
entities.tagline: Agents draft everything, inside conventions written down first, and I spend my time on the decisions they cannot make.

serves: Whoever decides about me decided from the model
upholds: Model it before you build it

sections.heading: The approach
sections.text:
AI drafts and it checks; it never decides and it never publishes. That is the position, and everything below exists to hold it: the constraint moved from building quickly to deciding correctly, so the scarce thing is judgment, and judgment is protected by making every decision leave a written artifact that a person put their name to. A fact enters the model from me or from a document, never from a model's recall, and nothing goes out under my name that I have not read against its sources.

A change of consequence starts as a written thing: a brief naming the audience and the facts it may claim, a spec that keeps the finding that led to the decision, then a plan. A smaller one still leaves a pull request, which is where its reason is written. Agents draft against those and against the schemas; I review on the branch, in the diff and on the rendered page. The conventions the agents work under are themselves files — how I write, how I work with git, what each repository is — vendored into every repository at a pinned release, so a rule improves in one place and reaches all of them. Roles are files too, in `model/roles/`: one seat held by me and every other by an agent, each saying what it takes, what it produces and what it never does. The Implementer commits what its brief specifies and never on its own initiative; none of the other agent-held seats commits at all.

Checks carry the load I would otherwise carry by reading. An unresolvable reference is an error rather than a warning, a pin that drifts fails a build, and the instance checker ends by naming what it did not reach — because the failure mode of an agent-written repository is a green check over an unread claim.

sections.heading: What it rules out
sections.text: No agent commits on its own initiative, and no agent merges at all. Work that leaves no artifact is not done: a decision reached in conversation and never written to a spec will be re-opened, so the conversation is not where it lives. Nothing is hand-maintained that could be derived — a second copy of a fact is the thing this model exists to end. No tool enters the chain before the convention it works under is written, because a tool adopted first sets the rules by what it happens to do. And no fact reaches a published surface because a model produced it fluently: a claim arrives from me or from a document or it does not arrive, and an agent that cannot find its source says so instead of writing around the gap.

sections.heading: What would show it is working
sections.text: A change to a published surface that bypassed the path — hand-edited, no spec, no pull request — is countable in git, and it has been zero since this strategy was adopted. A correction made twice is countable the same way: if the same fact has to be fixed in two places, a derivation is missing and the model has grown a second master. Both are visible the week they happen, which is the point; a strategy about how the work is done cannot wait for the horizon to be judged.

entities.name: blust.ch website
entities.tagline: The owner's own site, in English and Swiss Standard German, that a visitor, a search engine or an agent reaches at the owner's address, rebuilt from a pinned commit of the model.

sections.heading: What it shows
sections.text:
- **Home** — the profile's tagline, the identity's name, and the way into the talks and the ideas.
- **Team** — the process's phases as a board of the roles that own, execute, support and
  approve each, and the profiles that hold those roles.
- **Principles** — the vision and the values.
- **Surfaces** — every surface the model records and how each is made, by hand or by a build
  that reads a pinned commit.
- **Ideas** — the profile's ongoing community experiences that are open core, each with what it has shipped, which part is open and which one part could earn, and the questions their validation has to answer.
- **Model** — the company of one, drawn: the model's entities and edges as a graph from `model.json`.
- **Timeline** — the profile's experiences, drawn from `model.json`.
- **Talks** — the narrated talks this site serves, each an experience of the profile, in both languages with a PDF.
- **Privacy** — what leaves a visitor's browser and what stays in it, listed in full.
- **model.json** — the parsed model at the pinned commit, published as a dataset.
- **Chat** — the button at the foot of every prose page and the panel it opens, answered by the chat.blust.ch chat.
- **Structured data** — the person, the dataset and the site that every page describes to a
  crawler, with the person's addresses from the profile's `## Also at`.

sections.heading: Constraints
sections.text:
- The site collects nothing: no page sets a cookie, no page loads an analytics script, and
  nothing counts a visit.
- Every request a page makes on its own goes to the site's own origin; the one request to
  another address is the chat's, and only after the visitor has pressed send.
- Everything a page keeps in the browser is named on the privacy page, with its key and what
  it holds.

entities.name: chat.blust.ch chat
entities.tagline: The chat a visitor opens on blust.ch to ask about the owner's work, answered from what the mcp.blust.ch MCP server says at its pinned commit, and the page a person reaches at the same address.

sections.heading: What it shows
sections.text:
- **Endpoint** — `/chat` on this address, which a page of blust.ch posts a visitor's conversation to and which answers it as a stream of events.
- **Answer** — the text a language model writes from what the MCP server's tools returned for the visitor's question, in the language of the visitor's message, naming the entity each claim rests on.
- **From the model** — a link to each entity a tool returned on its own, opening it on the model page of blust.ch.
- **Refusals** — the sentences a visitor reads instead of an answer when the day's or the month's share is spent, when one address has sent too many messages in an hour, when the host does not answer or when the chat is switched off.
- **Page** — what a browser gets at the chat's own address: the host's name, the vision's and the identity's taglines, the paths and the events the endpoint answers, the fence that bounds what it spends, and the commit of the model it answers from.

entities.name: LinkedIn profile
entities.tagline: The professional network profile a recruiter, a client or a former colleague reaches first, kept by hand.

sections.heading: What it shows
sections.text:
- **Headline** — the profile's tagline, and nothing beside it.
- **Location** — the metropolitan area the network's own list offers for the identity's
  `location`.
- **About** — the profile's `## Summary`, rewritten in this surface's register.
- **Experience** — the experiences of kind `Role`, kind `Independent` and kind `Community`.
- **Projects** — the experiences of kind `Project`.
- **Education** — the experiences of kind `Education`.
- **Skills** — skills of the profile's, chosen by the owner.
- **Languages** — the languages `conventions/WRITING.md` names.

sections.heading: Projection rules
sections.text:
- Everything written for this surface is in the prose register of `conventions/WRITING.md`,
  aimed at a visitor who has not decided to stay.
- An entry's body is written rather than copied. What the experience holds was written for a
  reader who came to read, and this surface is read by one who has not decided to.
- An entry names the part played and the employer it was held through, where the model holds
  them. The part is the experience's `role`, and the employer is the `organization` of the
  containing period of kind `Role`, since that is the kind that names an employer; where no such
  period contains it, or more than one does, the entry names no employer. It reaches only a unit
  with somewhere to put it: a qualification names the body that issued it and never an employer,
  which the model does not say paid for it or knew of it. Both reach the entry,
  because a part named beside a client and not beside
  its employer reads as though the client employed you. An experience carrying no `role` shows
  none: its H1 is the part, or the model does not say.
- A body is written from the experience's `## Achievements`, and from its `## Ending` where the
  ending states a fact the achievements do not. An ending says why a period closed and what it
  left, and on some entries that is the only place the outcome is written down.
- The model is a company of one, so an experience nobody commissioned or hosted was the
  company's own work: an entry whose experience carries no `organization` names the identity,
  unless the kind says there was none. `Independent` says exactly that, so such an entry names no
  company, and the network's demand goes unmet rather than answered with a fact the model denies.
- An entry's body is one paragraph of at most three sentences, and where an ending is carried it
  is a second paragraph of one sentence. An entry whose period is a single day or a single month
  is one sentence and no second paragraph. A reader takes the first sentence and skims the rest,
  and a paragraph with no bound grows to the length of what an entry has to say rather than the
  length a reader will give it.
- Three sentences is a budget, and it is spent on what a recruiter, a client or a former
  colleague could not have guessed from the title. Prefer the achievement carrying a number, a
  named system or a named result over the one stating what was owned, since the schema already
  separates those and the title has said the second already. Where two carry evidence, the one a
  reader of this surface can act on wins: what was delivered and what changed, over how it was
  built.
- A sentence is not spent repeating another unit's wording or its detail. A summary claim that
  entries then evidence is not a repetition, it is what an About is for; two entries telling the
  same fact at the same length is.
- A sentence in a body carries one idea, as an achievement does, and runs to about twenty words.
  Three sentences each carrying five facts is the same wall as one unbounded paragraph with the
  breaks moved, and bounding the count without bounding the sentence is how a body gets there.
- For a talk, an article or a published tool the address is most of what the entry is, so an
  entry whose experience carries a `url` shows it. An entry whose experience carries none shows
  no link: the model holds an address or it does not, and this surface invents none.
- The sentence of the `## Summary` naming the security and compliance standards is not carried
  into the About text. A standard named without the work that met it is a claim the reader
  cannot place, and the About has no room to bring the work with it. The claim that sentence
  also makes about AI goes with it and is not restored: the headline is that claim.
- Every dated unit runs newest first by `end`, with an experience that has none — a period still
  running — above them all, and `start` breaking a tie. Not by `start`: a position starts once
  and then runs for years, so ordering by it buries a long role under everything that began
  while it was running, and a talk given during a job would stand above the job. What a reader
  wants first is what ended last. Where `end` and `start` both tie, the entry whose name sorts
  first in English comes first: an arbitrary choice, written down so that two producers make the
  same profile rather than each making one.
- Which unit takes an experience depends only on its kind. Every kind reaches one and none
  reaches two, so no experience is left over and none is shown twice.
- The Skills unit takes five because the network shows five on this account, and which five is
  the owner's because nothing here could derive them: the model holds far more skills than the
  unit shows and no ordering among them, so any five this surface chose would be a ranking it
  invented.
- The headline is the tagline and nothing beside it, so it carries no role, domain, project or
  location to resolve the name. That is a decision and this records its cost: the name is shared
  with a notable deceased academic, and a reader meeting the headline alone learns that this
  subject builds software, not what or where.
- The Languages unit takes the languages `conventions/WRITING.md` names. That is not a
  publishing habit standing in for a fact about a person: the conventions name the second
  because the person behind the family is Swiss, so the list is grounded in the subject and this
  unit reads it from there.
- The Skills unit carries no proficiency level. The surface shows names alone, and a level
  beside a name the surface does not explain reads as a grade.
- The tagline the headline carries states the claim this work makes rather than describing it,
  which core admits since 0.17.0 on one condition: the claim is one the model keeps elsewhere.
  This one is, as the value Decide well over build fast, so a reader who wants the argument
  behind the line has somewhere to go, and so the headline resolves the name through its subject
  rather than through a title.
- The model's values and its vision reach no unit of their own. The headline carries one
  value's claim, in the tagline's words, and nothing else on this surface states a principle.
- An experience's `## References` and its `skills` reach no unit either. The references are the
  documents a claim rests on, which a reader of the model follows and a reader of a profile does
  not — the entry's own address is what they came for. The skills are already on the surface, as
  the five the Skills unit carries, and a list per entry would be the same claim told longer.
- Nothing else the model holds reaches this surface: the standing links of the profile's
  `## Also at`, the identity's `email`, the experience kinds, the sources and this file's own
  type. Each is either how the model is kept, or a way to reach the
  subject that the network already provides.

sections.heading: Constraints
sections.text:
- The headline is at most 220 characters, the network's limit, read from its editor on
  2026-09-09.
- The About section is at most 2600 characters, read from the same editor on the same day.
- Every dated entry carries as its title the H1 of the experience it was made from, and the
  dates it shows are that experience's `start` and `end`. An experience with no `end` is a
  period still running, and its entry shows the start and no end date.
- Every name in the Skills unit is a skill in the model, spelled as that skill's H1.

entities.name: mcp.blust.ch MCP server
entities.tagline: The server an agent connects to for answers about the owner's work, and the page a person reaches at the same address, reading a pinned commit of the model and adding nothing to it.

sections.heading: What it shows
sections.text:
- **Endpoint** — `/mcp` on this address, the only path that speaks the protocol and the one a
  client is given. The registry listing's remote is this.
- **Title** — the identity's name.
- **Instructions** — the vision's tagline and the identity's tagline, then one sentence saying
  that every answer names the commit it was read from, and no commit of their own.
- **Tools** — listing the types, describing a schema, what the types declare about each other
  and what they constrain, the rules the model is held to and the checks that hold it, listing
  and returning entities, finding evidence, searching and fetching, over every entity in the
  model.
- **Page** — what a browser gets at the server's own address, for a reader who arrived at a
  protocol endpoint without a client: the identity's name, the vision's and the identity's
  taglines, the address to give a client, every tool with what it returns, and the commit the
  answers are read from.
- **Structured data** — the person and the endpoint that the page describes to a crawler, with
  the person's addresses from the profile's `## Also at`.

entities.name: MCP Registry listing
entities.tagline: The entry an agent client finds when it searches the public MCP Registry, pointing it at the MCP server.

sections.heading: What it shows
sections.text:
- **Title** — the identity's name.
- **Description** — the identity's name and the vision's name, joined by a colon.
- **Remote** — the MCP server's address.

entities.name: Build the alternative before making the point
entities.tagline: Naming what is broken is free, so it is not a position until something works differently.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text:
I do not publish a criticism until I have built the thing that answers it, and then the working alternative is what I lead with — the argument comes second and can be lost without the point collapsing. Where I cannot build it, I say the problem is real and leave the criticism unmade.

I never let a complaint stand as a position.

entities.name: Decide well over build fast
entities.tagline: AI moved the constraint from building quickly to deciding correctly; the decision is the work.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text:
I write the decision down before the code — with the alternatives that lost and why — so the next person can disagree with a reason rather than a rewrite. I spend the time that fast building saves on choosing well, because the constraint moved there.

I never ship a feature in a day and argue about it for a quarter because nobody can say what it was for.

entities.name: Grow the people with the platform
entities.tagline: A platform that outgrows the team that runs it is a liability with good uptime.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text:
I grow the organization as deliberately as the platform — hiring, practices, ownership — so that every part of the system has someone who could be woken up for it and would know what to do. I judge a platform by the team that can run it without me.

I never let five people know everything while twenty wait for them.

entities.name: Model it before you build it
entities.tagline: A business described as concepts and capabilities is one that people and AI can both act inside of.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text:
I keep a written model — domains, capabilities, processes, rules — that the code, the org chart and the agents all refer back to, and I keep it where the people who own the facts can edit it. I build from the model, not beside it. A project is decided before it is built, in how precisely its problem was described, and my talks on deciding well argue that from different angles.

I never let the model live in three heads and a slide deck, with every system encoding a slightly different version of it.

entities.name: Production is the finish line
entities.tagline: A platform counts when it runs for customers under real security and compliance obligations, not when the demo works.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text:
I own reliability, incident management and the audit trail as part of building the thing. I treat ISO 27001 and GDPR as design inputs, not a form to fill in after. I call it done when it runs for customers under real obligations, not when the demo works.

I never meet a launch date with a system nobody is on call for.

entities.name: One model, true everywhere
entities.tagline: Whoever asks about my work — a person, a search engine, an agent — reaches the same answer, because every surface they can reach derives from one model I keep, and no claim in it stands without its evidence.

sections.heading: What it means
sections.text:
Everything public about my work is derived rather than maintained. One model holds the facts: what I have built, the capabilities I claim with their evidence and what I hold to. The CV and its per-application dossiers, the website and its talks, the LinkedIn profile and the loadable skill bundle are outputs of it. When two of them disagree the model is what gets corrected and the surfaces are rebuilt; none of them is edited on its own.

The claim is not that any single surface is good. It is that they agree — because someone asking about me increasingly asks a machine, and a machine assembling an answer from contradictory sources produces either mush or a confident error. I would know this holds when the same question put to a person, to a search engine and to an agent comes back the same.

The scope is the work. Private life is out of scope by design rather than by omission: the schemas have nowhere to put it, which is a stronger guarantee than a promise.
